intro: For hundreds of years, most Europeans were born into a rank they could not easily leave. A serf's child became a serf. A noble's child became a noble. Then plague, towns, revolutions and machines began to shake that order loose. In this unit you will follow those changes from the medieval manor to the industrial city.

You will meet knights swearing oaths, barons facing down a king, and French commoners swearing an oath on a tennis court. You will stand inside a Manchester cotton mill and read the words of Adam Smith, Karl Marx and their critics. Each group saw fairness in its own way, and you will hear from all of them.

By the end, you will be able to explain how social class worked in Europe, name the events that changed it, and compare big ideas about work and wealth. You will use evidence to make your own claim, and you will treat people who disagree with care.
bigQuestion: What decides a person's place in society, and how have people worked to change it?

title: Social Class in Europe

chapters.title: Feudalism and the Three Estates
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a society built on fixed ranks slowly change, and what finally broke it apart?

story.title: The Oath on the Tennis Court
story.kicker: In June 1789, locked out of their meeting hall, hundreds of French commoners made a promise that shook a kingdom.
paragraphs: On the morning of June 20, 1789, a crowd of men in plain black coats walked through the rain at Versailles, outside Paris. They were deputies of the Third Estate, the group that spoke for ordinary French people. They came to their meeting hall and found the doors shut. Soldiers stood guard. Workmen said the room was being made ready for a royal ceremony.

The deputies had reason to worry. King Louis XVI had called the Estates-General, an old assembly of the three ranks of French society. It had not met since 1614. The clergy and the nobles each voted as one group. So did the commoners. Two groups could outvote the third every time, even though the commoners were almost the whole nation.

Someone remembered a big indoor court nearby, where nobles played an early form of tennis. The deputies crowded inside. There were no seats worth mentioning, only bare walls and a wooden floor. Their leader, an astronomer named Jean-Sylvain Bailly, stood on a table. One by one, the deputies swore not to separate until France had a written constitution.

Only one man refused to sign. Everyone else raised a hand or signed the paper. A few days later, some clergy and nobles joined them. Within weeks, Paris rose up and the old order began to fall. The system of three estates had lasted for centuries. On a tennis court, it began to end.
story.think: Why might a room and a locked door matter so much to people who felt they had no real voice?

lessons.title: Oaths, Lords and Vassals
lessons.mainIdea: Feudalism was a system where land was given in return for loyalty and military service.
reading: Picture a knight kneeling before a great lord in a stone hall around the year 1100. The knight puts his hands between the lord's hands. He promises to be the lord's man and to fight for him. The lord promises to protect him. Then the lord hands him a clod of earth or a stick, a sign that the knight now holds a piece of land.

This bond is what historians call *feudalism*. The lord gave land to a follower. The follower who received it was a *vassal*. The land itself was a *fief*. In return, the vassal owed loyalty, advice and usually about forty days of fighting each year. The promise of loyalty was called fealty, and it was sworn on holy objects.

Feudalism grew in western Europe after the empire of Charlemagne broke apart in the 800s. Kings were weak and raiders were strong. Local lords with armed followers kept order where they could. The system was never exactly the same everywhere. Many historians today say 'feudalism' is a tidy label for a messy set of local customs.

words.d: a system in medieval Europe where land was given in exchange for loyalty and military service
a person who received land from a lord and promised him loyalty and service
the land a lord granted to a vassal

look.title: A Chain of Promises
look.text: A king grants a large region to a duke. The duke grants part of it to a count. The count grants a village to a knight. Each man kneels to the one above him and swears loyalty. Each one promises to protect the one below him.
look.prompt: Who does the knight owe loyalty to directly? What could go wrong if the duke and the king quarrel?

choices: A fief, or grant of land
A salary paid in gold coins
A share of a trading company
check.why: The reading says the land a lord gave to a vassal was called a fief.

check.q: What did a vassal owe his lord in return?
choices: Only a yearly tax in money
A promise to become a priest

check.q: Why did feudalism grow after the 800s in western Europe?
choices: The Roman Empire had just been founded
Kings were weak and local lords kept order against raiders
Merchants had taken over every city
check.why: After Charlemagne's empire broke apart, local lords with armed followers kept order where kings could not.

lessons.title: Life on the Manor
lessons.mainIdea: Most medieval people were peasants who farmed a lord's manor, and many were serfs tied to the land.
reading: Imagine a village in England around 1250. There is a stone manor house, a church, a mill, and cottages of wood and mud. Around them stretch long strips of plowed field. The lord of the village owns all of it. Historians call this unit of land and people a *manor*.

Most families on a manor were peasants, and many were *serfs*. A serf was not a slave. He could not be sold away from his family, and he had his own strip of land to farm. But he could not leave the manor without the lord's permission. He owed the lord work on the lord's own fields, often a few days a week, and paid fees to use the lord's mill and oven.

Serfs lived hard lives, but they were not helpless. Villages had customs that even a lord was expected to respect. Peasants took disputes to the manor court. Over time, many serfs bought their freedom or ran away to towns. Life was different from place to place, and some peasants were free farmers from the start.

words.d: a lord's estate, including his house, farmland, village and the people who worked there
a peasant who was bound to a lord's land and owed him labor, but was not owned like a slave

look.title: A Serf's Week
look.text: Monday to Wednesday, Alice's father plows the lord's fields. Thursday and Friday he works his own family strips. On Saturday the family grinds grain at the lord's mill and pays part of the flour as a fee. On Sunday they go to church and pay part of their harvest to the priest.
look.prompt: How many days did the family work only for themselves? What does that tell you about who gained most from their work?

check.q: How was a serf different from a slave?
choices: A serf could leave the manor whenever he wanted
A serf owned the manor house
A serf never had to work for the lord
A serf could not be sold apart from family and had land to farm
check.why: The reading says a serf could not be sold away from his family and had his own strip of land.

check.q: What did a serf owe the lord?
choices: Work on the lord's fields and fees for the mill and oven
Forty days of service as a knight
A tenth of all town trade
check.why: Serfs worked the lord's fields, often a few days a week, and paid fees to use his mill and oven.

check.q: Which statement about serfs is supported by the reading?
choices: They had no customs or courts
Some bought their freedom or ran to towns
They were all exactly alike everywhere
check.why: The reading says many serfs bought their freedom or ran away to towns, and villages had courts and customs.

lessons.title: The Church at the Center
lessons.mainIdea: The Catholic Church shaped daily life, owned great amounts of land, and collected a tithe from almost everyone.
reading: In a medieval village, the tallest building was usually the church. Its bell marked the hours of work and prayer. Babies were baptized there, couples married there, and the dead were buried beside it. For most western Europeans, the Catholic Church gave life its meaning and its calendar of feasts and holy days.

The Church was also rich and powerful. Bishops and abbots controlled huge estates, often with their own serfs. Almost everyone paid a *tithe*, one tenth of their harvest or income, to support the Church. Monasteries copied books, ran schools and cared for the sick and the poor.

People inside the Church often argued about its wealth. Francis of Assisi, in the early 1200s, gave up his family's riches and asked his followers to live in poverty. Critics then and later said some church leaders lived like nobles. Supporters pointed to the hospitals, schools and charity the Church provided.

words.d: a payment of one tenth of a person's harvest or income to support the Church
people ordained for religious work, such as priests, monks, nuns and bishops

look.title: Two Views of Church Wealth
look.text: View A: The Church owns great estates, so it can run hospitals, feed the poor and copy books. View B: Friar Francis says followers of Jesus should own nothing, and that riches pull church leaders away from the poor.
look.prompt: What does each view care about most? Could a person agree with parts of both?

check.q: What was a tithe?
choices: A fee paid to use the lord's mill
A tax paid by merchants to a guild
One tenth of a harvest or income given to the Church
check.why: A tithe was one tenth of a person's harvest or income, paid to support the Church.

check.q: Which of these did monasteries do, according to the reading?
choices: Copied books and cared for the sick and poor
check.why: The reading says monasteries copied books, ran schools and cared for the sick and poor.

check.q: What did Francis of Assisi ask his followers to do?
check.why: Francis gave up his riches and asked his followers to live in poverty.

lessons.title: Those Who Pray, Fight and Work
lessons.mainIdea: Medieval writers described society as three orders, or estates: clergy, nobles and commoners.
reading: Around the year 1000, a few church writers described society with a simple picture. Some people pray. Some people fight. Some people work. Each group was supposed to serve the others, like parts of one body. This idea became the three *estates*.

The First Estate was the clergy, who prayed for everyone's souls. The Second Estate was the *nobility*, families who held land and fought as knights. The Third Estate was everyone else: peasants, craftsmen, merchants and later lawyers and bankers. The first two estates were small but held special rights, such as freedom from many taxes.

The picture was an ideal, not a photograph. A rich merchant and a poor serf were both in the Third Estate, yet their lives were very different. A younger son of a noble might become a bishop. Still, the idea of three orders lasted for centuries. In France it shaped law and taxes right up to 1789.

words.d: one of the three ranks of medieval and early modern European society
families with inherited titles, land and special legal rights

look.title: Three Kinds of People
look.text: The house of God is threefold. Here below, some pray, others fight, and still others work. The three belong together and cannot be separated.
look.cite: Adalbero, Bishop of Laon, poem to King Robert II of France, c. 1020s (paraphrase)
look.prompt: Why might a bishop like this picture of society? Who gets left out of the choice?

check.q: Which group was the First Estate?
check.why: The First Estate was the clergy, who prayed.

check.q: Why were a rich merchant and a poor serf in the same estate?
choices: Both were commoners, neither clergy nor noble
check.why: The Third Estate included everyone who was not clergy or noble, rich or poor.

check.q: According to Adalbero's picture, what was each estate supposed to do?
choices: Serve the others as part of one whole
check.why: The idea was that the three orders belonged together and served each other.

lessons.title: The Black Death
lessons.mainIdea: The plague of 1347–51 killed a huge share of Europe's people and left the survivors in a changed world.
reading: In 1347, ships from the Black Sea docked in Sicily. Soon people in the port were falling sick with fever and painful swellings. Within four years, the disease had swept across nearly all of Europe. People later called it the *Black Death*.

Today scientists know the cause was a germ called Yersinia pestis, spread by fleas on rats and, some researchers think, from person to person. People at the time did not know about germs. Some blamed bad air. Some saw punishment from God. In many towns, angry crowds blamed Jewish neighbors and murdered them, a terrible crime against innocent people.

Historians disagree on exact numbers. Most say that between about one third and one half of Europe's people died. Some villages were emptied. Whole families vanished. Survivors faced a world with far fewer hands to plant crops, weave cloth and build walls.

words.d: the great plague that swept Europe from 1347 to 1351 and killed a huge share of its people
a deadly disease that spreads widely; here, the disease caused by the germ Yersinia pestis

look.title: How Many Died?
look.unit: percent of Europe's people who died
look.cite: Range of historians' estimates; Ole J. Benedictow, The Black Death 1346–1353: The Complete History (2004)
look.prompt: Why do you think historians give a range instead of one exact number?

check.q: When did the Black Death sweep across Europe?
check.why: The reading dates the plague from 1347 to 1351.

check.q: What do scientists today say caused the Black Death?
check.why: Scientists identify the germ Yersinia pestis, spread by fleas on rats.

check.q: Why do the numbers in the table differ?
choices: Historians estimate differently because records are incomplete
check.why: The reading says historians disagree on exact numbers, so they give a range.

lessons.title: Workers After the Plague
lessons.mainIdea: With so many dead, surviving workers asked for higher pay, and lords tried hard to stop them.
reading: After the plague, a lord in England might find half his fields empty. The peasants who were left knew their work was now precious. They asked for higher wages. If one lord said no, they could move to a manor that said yes. This is a *labor shortage*: too few workers for the work that needs doing.

Lords and kings pushed back. In 1351 the English Parliament passed the Statute of Labourers. It tried to hold wages at the level they had been before the plague. Many workers ignored it, and many lords broke it quietly to keep their fields farmed.

Anger grew. In 1381, peasants in England rose up in what is called the Peasants' Revolt. Led by Wat Tyler and a priest named John Ball, they marched on London. The revolt was crushed and Tyler was killed. Yet over the next century, serfdom slowly faded in England, as lords found it easier to rent land or pay workers.

words.d: a time when there are too few workers for the work that needs to be done
an uprising by people against those who rule them

look.title: A Priest's Question
look.text: When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then the gentleman?
look.cite: Rhyme linked to John Ball's sermon during the Peasants' Revolt, 1381, as reported by chroniclers
look.prompt: Delved means dug; span means spun thread. What is the rhyme saying about nobles?

check.q: Why could peasants ask for higher wages after the plague?
choices: So many had died that workers were scarce
check.why: A labor shortage made the surviving workers' labor precious.

check.q: What did the Statute of Labourers of 1351 try to do?
choices: Hold wages at the level before the plague
check.why: The statute tried to keep wages at pre-plague levels.

check.q: Who led the Peasants' Revolt of 1381?
check.why: The reading names Wat Tyler and the priest John Ball as leaders.

sections.title: Limits on Kings, Freedom in Towns

lessons.title: Magna Carta
lessons.mainIdea: In 1215 English barons forced King John to accept Magna Carta, which said even a king must follow the law.
reading: In June 1215, King John of England rode to a meadow called Runnymede, beside the River Thames. Waiting for him were barons, powerful nobles who were furious. John had lost wars in France and squeezed them for money again and again. They had taken up arms, and London had opened its gates to them.

At Runnymede the king agreed to a long list of promises. The document became known as *Magna Carta*, Latin for 'Great Charter'. One famous clause said no free man could be jailed or have his property taken except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land. The idea that the ruler is bound by law is called the *rule of law*.

Magna Carta was mainly a deal between a king and nobles. Most of its promises did not help serfs. John quickly got the Pope to cancel it, and war followed. But later kings reissued it, and over centuries people used it to argue that no ruler is above the law. Its ideas later influenced the United States Constitution.

words.d: the 'Great Charter' of 1215 that limited the power of King John of England
the idea that everyone, including rulers, must follow the law
a powerful noble who held land directly from the king

look.title: Clause 39
look.text: No free man shall be seized or imprisoned, or stripped of his rights or possessions, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
look.cite: Magna Carta, clause 39, 1215 (modern English translation, British Library)
look.prompt: Who does this clause protect, and who does the phrase 'free man' leave out?

check.q: Who forced King John to accept Magna Carta?
check.why: Powerful nobles called barons took up arms and forced the king to agree.

check.q: What does 'rule of law' mean?
choices: The king makes any law he likes
Everyone, even the ruler, must follow the law
check.why: Rule of law means rulers are bound by law too.

check.q: Why did Magna Carta do little for serfs at first?
choices: It was mainly a deal between the king and nobles
check.why: The reading says it was mainly a deal between a king and nobles, and its promises protected 'free men'.

lessons.title: Towns, Guilds and Merchants
lessons.mainIdea: Growing towns gave merchants and craftsmen a new kind of life outside the manor, organized by guilds.
reading: By the 1200s, towns like Florence, Paris, Bruges and London were bustling. Walls ringed markets full of cloth, spices, wool and wine. Many towns won charters from kings or lords that let them govern themselves. A serf who ran to a town and lived there a year and a day could often claim his freedom. A German saying held that 'town air makes you free'.

Inside towns, craftsmen organized *guilds*. A guild was an association of people in one trade, such as bakers or weavers. It set prices, standards and training. A boy began as an *apprentice*, living with a master for years. Next he became a journeyman who worked for wages. If he made a fine 'masterpiece', he could become a master himself.

Merchants grew rich, and some became richer than nobles. Yet they still belonged to the Third Estate. Guilds protected members but also kept outsiders out, and women's work was often limited, though some widows ran their husbands' shops. Towns showed that a person could rise through work and trade, not only through birth.

words.d: an association of craftsmen or merchants in one trade that set rules, prices and training
a young person learning a trade by working for a master for several years
a written grant of rights, such as the right of a town to govern itself

look.title: From Apprentice to Master
look.text: Age 12: Pieter moves in with a master weaver in Bruges. Age 19: he finishes his training and works for wages in several shops. Age 26: he weaves a fine piece of cloth and shows it to the guild's leaders. They approve it, and he opens his own shop.
look.prompt: Name the three stages Pieter passed through. What role did the guild play at each step?

check.q: What was a guild?
choices: An association of people in one trade
check.why: A guild organized people in one trade and set prices, standards and training.

check.q: What was the step between apprentice and master?
check.why: After training, an apprentice became a journeyman who worked for wages.

check.q: What did 'town air makes you free' refer to?
choices: Towns had cleaner air than farms
Towns paid no taxes to anyone
A serf living in a town for a year and a day could claim freedom
check.why: The saying referred to serfs gaining freedom by living in a town for a year and a day.

lessons.title: A Kingdom in Crisis
lessons.mainIdea: By 1789 France was deep in debt, bread was expensive, and the Third Estate paid most of the taxes.
reading: In the spring of 1789, a loaf of bread in Paris could cost more than half a worker's daily pay. A bad harvest the year before had pushed prices up. At the same time, the French government was nearly broke. It had spent heavily on wars, including helping the Americans win independence from Britain.

The burden fell unevenly. Nobles and clergy were free from many taxes. Peasants paid taxes to the king, dues to lords and tithes to the Church. Educated members of the Third Estate, such as lawyers and doctors, resented being treated as lesser people. Many had read writers of the Enlightenment, who argued that people have natural rights.

To raise money, Louis XVI called the Estates-General for May 1789. A priest named Emmanuel Sieyès wrote a famous pamphlet asking, 'What is the Third Estate?' His answer was that it was everything, yet it had been treated as nothing. The pamphlet spread quickly and gave commoners a new sense of their own importance.

words.d: the assembly of representatives of France's three estates, called by the king
an 18th-century movement of thinkers who stressed reason and natural rights

look.title: Who Were the French in 1789?
look.cite: Common estimates; see William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (1989)
look.prompt: If each estate got one vote, how much of the population could the first two estates outvote?

check.q: Why did Louis XVI call the Estates-General in 1789?
choices: He wanted to free the serfs
He wanted to end the monarchy
check.why: The government was nearly broke, so the king called the assembly to raise money.

check.q: What was Sieyès's argument?
choices: The Third Estate was everything but treated as nothing
The Church should collect more tithes
check.why: Sieyès's pamphlet said the Third Estate was everything, yet treated as nothing.

check.q: According to the table, about what share of French people were in the Third Estate?
check.why: The table shows the Third Estate as about 98 percent of the population.

lessons.title: The Old Order Falls
lessons.mainIdea: In 1789 the National Assembly ended noble privileges and declared that people are born free and equal in rights.
reading: After the Tennis Court Oath, the Third Estate called itself the *National Assembly*. It claimed to speak for the whole nation. On July 14, 1789, crowds in Paris stormed the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison. In the countryside, frightened and angry peasants attacked lords' manor houses and burned the records of their dues.

On the night of August 4, 1789, members of the Assembly stood up one after another and gave up old privileges. Nobles' special rights, church tithes and many feudal dues were ended. Legally, the three estates were gone. Every French man was now a citizen under one law.

Weeks later, on August 26, the Assembly approved the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its first article said men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Critics noted it did not give women equal rights. The writer Olympe de Gouges answered in 1791 with a declaration of the rights of woman.

words.d: the body formed by the Third Estate in June 1789 to write a constitution for France
a special right or freedom given to one group and not to others
a member of a nation with rights and duties under its laws

look.title: Article 1
look.text: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be based only on common usefulness.
look.cite: Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, Article 1, France, 1789 (English translation)
look.prompt: How does this article reject the idea of three estates?

check.q: What happened on the night of August 4, 1789?
choices: The Assembly ended noble privileges and many feudal dues
check.why: On August 4, members gave up old privileges, ending the estates in law.

check.q: What was the Bastille?
choices: A royal fortress and prison in Paris
check.why: The Bastille was a royal fortress and prison stormed on July 14, 1789.

check.q: What criticism did Olympe de Gouges make?
choices: The declaration gave nobles too few rights
The rights declared did not include women equally
France should keep the three estates
The king should rule without law
check.why: She wrote a declaration of the rights of woman because the 1789 declaration left women out of equal rights.

lessons.title: Hope and Terror
lessons.mainIdea: The Revolution ended legal ranks, but it also turned violent, and people still argue about its meaning.
reading: The Revolution did not stop in 1789. In 1792 France became a republic, and in January 1793 Louis XVI was executed. War broke out with neighboring kingdoms. A group led by Maximilien Robespierre took control and began what is called the *Reign of Terror*. Suspected enemies were tried quickly and sent to the guillotine.

Historians commonly count about 17,000 official death sentences during the Terror, and many more people died in prisons and in fighting inside France. Robespierre himself was executed in 1794. Years later, in 1799, the general Napoleon Bonaparte seized power.

People have argued about the Revolution ever since. Supporters say it ended feudal privilege and spread the ideas of equal citizens and rights. The British writer Edmund Burke warned in 1790 that tearing down old customs all at once would lead to chaos and tyranny. Many historians say both sides point to something real.

words.d: the period of 1793–94 in revolutionary France when thousands of suspected enemies were executed
a government with no king, where leaders are chosen by citizens

look.title: Two Verdicts
look.text: Voice 1: The Revolution swept away privilege by birth. After it, a baker's son and a duke's son stood equal before the law. Voice 2: The Revolution tore up the old order so fast that fear took over. Thousands died, and it ended with a general in charge.
look.prompt: Which facts from the lesson support each voice? Is there a way both could be partly right?

check.q: What was the Reign of Terror?
choices: A period when thousands of suspected enemies were executed
A peaceful vote to end the estates
check.why: During the Terror of 1793–94, suspected enemies were tried quickly and executed.

check.q: What did Edmund Burke warn in 1790?
choices: The Terror was a good idea
Tearing down customs all at once would lead to chaos
check.why: Burke warned that sudden change would lead to chaos and tyranny.

check.q: Who seized power in France in 1799?
check.why: The reading says Napoleon Bonaparte seized power in 1799.

review.q: In feudalism, what was a fief?
choices: Land granted by a lord to a vassal
review.why: A fief was the land a lord granted in return for loyalty and service.

review.q: Which group belonged to the Second Estate?
review.why: The Second Estate was the nobility, who held land and fought.

review.q: How did the Black Death change life for surviving workers?
choices: Workers were scarce, so they could ask for higher pay
review.why: The labor shortage made workers' labor more valuable.

review.q: What main idea is Magna Carta remembered for?
choices: Even a king must follow the law
Kings rule by divine right with no limits
All people are equal in every way
review.why: Magna Carta is remembered for putting the king under the law.

review.q: How did towns offer serfs a way out of serfdom?
choices: A serf who lived in a town a year and a day could often claim freedom
The Church freed serfs in towns
review.why: Many town charters allowed a serf living there a year and a day to claim freedom.

review.q: Why did the Third Estate meet on a tennis court in June 1789?
choices: The king invited them to play
They were locked out of their meeting hall
review.why: The story tells how deputies found their hall locked and met at a nearby indoor court.

review.q: What ended the three estates in French law?
choices: The decisions of the night of August 4, 1789
review.why: On August 4, 1789, the Assembly ended noble privileges and feudal dues.

review.q: Compare the Peasants' Revolt and the French Revolution. What is one difference?
choices: The Peasants' Revolt was crushed; the French Revolution ended legal ranks
Only the Peasants' Revolt ended serfdom at once
The French Revolution happened in England
review.why: The 1381 revolt was crushed, while the 1789 Revolution ended the estates in law.

chapters.title: Factories, Workers and the Middle Class
chapters.bigQuestion: When machines changed how people worked, who gained, who paid the cost, and how did societies respond?

story.title: The Piecer
story.kicker: In a Manchester cotton mill in the 1830s, a ten-year-old girl spends her day chasing broken threads.
paragraphs: The mill bell rings at half past five in the morning. Mary is ten years old. She pulls on her shawl and hurries through the dark streets of Manchester with hundreds of other workers. The air smells of coal smoke. Inside the mill, the noise of the spinning machines is so loud that people talk with their hands.

Mary's job is called piecing. The spinning machine, called a mule, rolls forward and back, twisting cotton into thread. When a thread snaps, Mary must reach in and twist the ends together before the machine rolls back. She is small, so she fits where adults cannot. She walks back and forth all day, and she must keep her fingers clear of the moving parts.

The workday lasts about twelve hours, with short breaks for meals. The overseer watches for anyone who slows down or dozes off. Cotton dust floats in the warm, damp air and settles in her hair and lungs. Mary earns only a few shillings a week, but her family needs every penny to pay rent and buy bread.

Mary is not one real girl. She stands for many thousands of children who worked in British mills in these years. In 1832 some of them told their stories to a committee of Parliament. What they said helped change the law, and it began a long debate about work, wealth and fairness that still goes on.
story.think: Mary's family needed her wages, but her work was long and dangerous. What choices did her family really have?

lessons.title: Why Britain Went First
lessons.mainIdea: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about the 1760s, helped by coal, capital, trade and new inventions.
reading: In 1700, almost all cloth in Britain was spun and woven by hand, often in family cottages. By 1850, much of it came from huge buildings full of machines. This great shift from hand tools to machines and factories is called the *Industrial Revolution*. It began in Britain from about the 1760s.

Historians point to several reasons Britain went first. It had lots of coal and iron close together. It had merchants and banks with money to invest, called *capital*. Its colonies and trade gave it raw cotton and markets for its goods. It also had inventors and tinkerers who kept improving machines.

One key invention was a better steam engine. In the 1760s and 1770s, James Watt improved earlier engines so they wasted far less fuel. Steam engines could pump water from mines and later run machines anywhere, not just beside rivers. Historians still debate how much each reason mattered, and some stress that raw cotton often came from enslaved labor in the Americas.

words.d: the shift, starting in Britain about the 1760s, from making goods by hand to making them with machines in factories
money or goods used to start or grow a business
a machine that uses the power of steam from boiling water to make things move

look.title: A Recipe for Industry
look.text: Ingredient 1: coal and iron in the ground. Ingredient 2: merchants with money to invest. Ingredient 3: raw cotton from trade and colonies. Ingredient 4: inventors who improve machines. Ingredient 5: customers at home and overseas.
look.prompt: Which ingredient do you think mattered most? Explain what would happen if it were missing.

check.q: What does 'capital' mean in this lesson?
choices: The main city of a country
Money or goods used to start or grow a business
check.why: Capital is money invested in business, which British merchants and banks had.

check.q: What did James Watt improve?
check.why: Watt improved the steam engine so it wasted far less fuel.

check.q: Which was one reason Britain industrialized first?
choices: It had no trade with other lands
It had coal and iron close together
check.why: The reading names coal and iron close together as one reason.

lessons.title: The Factory System
lessons.mainIdea: Factories brought workers and machines together under one roof, run by the clock.
reading: In 1771, Richard Arkwright opened a cotton-spinning mill at Cromford in Derbyshire. Its machines were driven by a water wheel. Hundreds of workers, many of them children, tended them in shifts. Arkwright is often called a founder of the *factory system*.

In the old way, a weaver worked at home and set her own hours. In a *factory*, the owner owned the machines and the building. Workers came at a fixed time and left at a fixed time. Bells and clocks ruled the day. A worker who came late could lose pay.

Factories could make cloth far faster and cheaper than hand workers. Prices of cotton goods fell, and ordinary people could afford more clothes. But many hand weavers lost their living. Some, called Luddites, smashed machines in the 1810s in protest. The government sent soldiers, and machine-breaking was made a crime punishable by death.

words.d: a building where workers use machines to make goods in large numbers
a way of making goods in which workers gather in one place to run machines owned by an employer

look.title: Home or Mill?
look.text: Before: Hannah spins at home by the fire. She can stop to feed the baby. She sells her thread to a merchant who visits each week. After: Hannah walks to the mill at dawn. The machines set the pace. She earns a steady wage, but she cannot leave until the bell rings.
look.prompt: What did Hannah gain and what did she lose by moving to the mill?

check.q: Who opened a water-powered spinning mill at Cromford in 1771?
check.why: Richard Arkwright opened the Cromford mill and is often called a founder of the factory system.

check.q: How was factory work different from home work?
choices: Workers kept fixed hours set by the owner and the clock
check.why: In factories, clocks and bells set the hours, and the owner owned the machines.

check.q: Who were the Luddites?
choices: Workers who smashed machines in protest
check.why: Luddites were workers who broke machines in the 1810s to protest losing their living.

lessons.title: Crowded Cities
lessons.mainIdea: Factories drew millions of people into fast-growing cities that were often crowded and unhealthy.
reading: Manchester was a modest market town in the mid-1700s. By 1851 it held about 300,000. People poured in from farms, and from Ireland, to find work in the mills. The growth of cities is called *urbanization*.

Builders threw up rows of cheap houses, packed tightly together. Many families lived in one room or a damp cellar. There were few sewers and little clean water. Diseases like cholera and typhus spread quickly. In the poorest districts, many children did not live to the age of five.

City life also brought new chances. There were shops, newspapers, chapels, and later libraries and schools. Reformers such as Edwin Chadwick, in a report of 1842, showed that dirty water and poor drains caused disease. Slowly, cities built sewers and water systems that saved many lives.

words.d: the growth of cities as people move from the countryside to towns
a person who works to improve laws or conditions

look.title: People in England and Wales
look.cite: Census of England and Wales, 1801, 1851 and 1901 (UK Office for National Statistics)
look.prompt: About how many times larger was the population in 1901 than in 1801?

check.q: What does 'urbanization' mean?
choices: Moving from cities to the countryside
The growth of cities as people move to towns
check.why: Urbanization is the growth of cities as people move from the countryside.

check.q: Why did disease spread in new industrial cities?
choices: Crowded homes had few sewers and little clean water
check.why: The reading links cholera and typhus to crowding, few sewers and dirty water.

check.q: According to the census table, about what was the population of England and Wales in 1851?
check.why: The table shows about 17.9 million people in 1851.

lessons.title: Children at Work
lessons.mainIdea: Children worked long hours in mills and mines, and their testimony helped change public opinion.
reading: Children had always worked on farms and in family shops. What changed in the factory age was the scale and the pace. In mills, children tied threads and crawled under machines to sweep. In coal mines, some children sat alone in the dark, opening and closing air doors for coal carts.

In 1832, a committee of Parliament led by Michael Sadler heard from mill workers. Many said they had started work at eight or younger. They told of twelve- to fourteen-hour days, beatings for being slow and injuries from machines. Critics then said Sadler chose the worst cases, and historians still discuss how typical they were.

Many parents sent children to work because families needed the wages to survive. Some mill owners argued that work kept children out of trouble. Others, like the reformer Lord Ashley (later the Earl of Shaftesbury), argued that children needed schooling and rest. This debate shaped laws on *child labor* for the rest of the century.

words.d: the work of children in jobs such as mills or mines, often long hours for low pay
a statement a person gives about what they have seen or lived through

look.title: A Mill Worker Remembers
look.text: A former mill girl told the committee she began work at about six years old. In busy times her days were far longer than twelve hours. When she was late or slow, she was strapped by the overseer.
look.cite: Testimony to the Select Committee on the Bill for the Regulation of Factories (Sadler Committee), British Parliament, 1832 (paraphrase)
look.prompt: What details make this testimony powerful? Why might a historian also want other sources?

check.q: What did the Sadler Committee of 1832 do?
choices: Heard testimony from mill workers about their conditions
check.why: The committee led by Michael Sadler heard workers describe long hours and harsh treatment.

check.q: Why did many parents send children to work?
choices: Families needed the wages to survive
check.why: The reading says families often needed children's wages to survive.

check.q: What criticism was made of the Sadler Committee?
choices: It may have chosen the worst cases
check.why: Critics said Sadler chose the worst cases, and historians still discuss how typical they were.

lessons.title: The Working Class
lessons.mainIdea: Factory workers who earned wages and owned no property became a new, large working class.
reading: In a medieval village, a serf was tied to a lord. In an industrial city, a worker was tied to a wage. People who lived by selling their labor for wages, and owned little else, came to be called the *working class*. By the mid-1800s they were the largest group in Britain's cities.

Work was often unsteady. When orders fell, mills cut hours or closed, and workers could be laid off with no help. There was no sick pay and no pension. Many families pooled wages from parents and children. Friendly societies, which members paid into each week, helped cover funerals and illness.

Workers built their own culture too. They founded chapels, reading rooms, choirs and cooperative shops. In 1844 a group of workers in Rochdale opened a cooperative store owned by its customers. Many workers also joined the Chartist movement of the 1830s and 1840s, which asked for the vote for all men.

words.d: people who earn their living mainly by selling their labor for wages
money paid to a worker for work done, usually by the hour, day or week
a business owned and run by its members, who share the profits

look.title: A Family Budget
look.text: Father earns 18 shillings a week at the mill. Mother earns 7 shillings. Their son, age 11, earns 3. Rent is 4 shillings. Bread and potatoes take most of the rest. When the mill cuts to three days a week, father's pay is halved.
look.prompt: What happens to this family's budget when father's pay is halved? What could they do?

check.q: Who made up the working class?
choices: People who lived mainly by selling their labor for wages
check.why: The working class lived by earning wages and owned little else.

check.q: What did friendly societies do?
choices: Helped members pay for illness and funerals
check.why: Members paid in each week, and the society helped with illness and funerals.

check.q: What did the Chartist movement ask for?
check.why: Chartists in the 1830s and 1840s asked for the vote for all men.

lessons.title: The Rising Middle Class
lessons.mainIdea: Factory owners, merchants and professionals formed a growing middle class with new wealth and influence.
reading: Picture a brick house on a quiet street at the edge of Manchester, far from the smoke. A mill owner lives here with his family and a servant or two. His children go to school. On Sunday the family attends chapel, and in the evening they read novels by the fire. This family belongs to the *middle class*.

The middle class included factory owners, merchants, bankers, doctors, lawyers, clerks and shopkeepers. They were not nobles, and most did not do manual work. Many valued hard work, saving, education and respectability. They saw themselves as people who had earned their place.

The middle class gained political power as well. The Reform Act of 1832 gave the vote to many middle-class men in Britain, though not to most workers. Some middle-class people gave to charity and pushed for reform. Critics said many ignored the poverty that made their wealth possible.

words.d: the social group between the wealthy upper class and the working class, such as owners, merchants and professionals
a British law that gave the vote to many middle-class men and changed how seats in Parliament were shared

look.title: Two Neighbors
look.text: Mr. Hale owns a mill and lives in a new brick house with a garden. His clerk, Mr. Price, earns a salary, rents a small house and hopes to send his son to a good school. Neither man was born noble. Neither works a machine.
look.prompt: Why might both men see themselves as middle class, even though one is much richer?

check.q: Which of these was usually part of the middle class?
check.why: The middle class included professionals such as doctors, and merchants.

check.q: What did the Reform Act of 1832 do?
choices: Gave the vote to all workers
Gave the vote to many middle-class men
check.why: The act gave the vote to many middle-class men, though not most workers.

check.q: What values did many middle-class people stress?
choices: Hard work, saving, education and respectability
check.why: The reading lists hard work, saving, education and respectability.

lessons.title: Trade Unions
lessons.mainIdea: Workers formed trade unions to bargain together for better pay and conditions, despite early bans.
reading: In 1834, six farm workers from the village of Tolpuddle in Dorset, England, formed a society. They wanted to resist wage cuts. They swore a secret oath together. For that oath, they were arrested and sentenced to be shipped to Australia. Crowds protested, and after about two years they were pardoned. They became known as the Tolpuddle Martyrs.

A *trade union* is a group of workers who join together to bargain with employers. One worker alone has little power. Many workers together can ask for better pay, shorter hours or safer conditions. If talks fail, they may go on *strike*, meaning they stop work together.

British law banned unions under the Combination Acts of 1799 and 1800, but these were repealed in 1824. Unions slowly grew and became legal and strong later in the century. Supporters said unions gave workers a fair voice. Critics, including many employers, said unions raised costs and limited a person's freedom to work on their own terms.

words.d: an organization of workers who join together to bargain with employers
when workers stop working together to press for better pay or conditions

look.title: Alone or Together?
look.text: Case A: One spinner asks the owner for a raise. The owner says, 'There are ten people at the gate who will take your job.' Case B: All two hundred spinners ask together and say they will stop work if refused.
look.prompt: Why might the owner answer differently in Case B? What risks do the workers take?

check.q: What is a trade union?
choices: A group of workers who bargain together with employers
check.why: A trade union is workers joining together to bargain with employers.

check.q: Why were the Tolpuddle Martyrs punished?
choices: They swore a secret oath when forming a workers' society
check.why: They were sentenced for swearing a secret oath while forming their society.

check.q: What is a strike?
choices: A factory owner closing a mill for good
Workers stopping work together to press their demands
check.why: A strike is when workers stop work together to press for better pay or conditions.

lessons.title: The Factory Acts
lessons.mainIdea: Britain passed Factory Acts that limited children's hours and sent inspectors to enforce the rules.
reading: After the Sadler Committee, Parliament acted. The Factory Act of 1833 said textile mills could not hire children under nine. Children aged nine to thirteen could work no more than nine hours a day. It also created paid *factory inspectors* to visit mills and enforce the law. Earlier laws had failed partly because no one checked.

More laws followed. The Mines Act of 1842 banned women, girls and boys under ten from working underground. The Factory Act of 1847, known as the Ten Hours Act, limited women and young people in textile mills to ten hours a day. Over time, rules spread to more industries.

The Factory Acts were debated hard. Supporters said the state must protect those who could not protect themselves. Opponents said the laws interfered with free contracts, raised costs and could hurt families who needed wages. The acts are an early example of *regulation*: government rules for how businesses operate.

words.d: British laws of the 1800s that limited working hours and set conditions in factories
a government official who visits workplaces to check that the law is followed
a rule made by government to control how businesses or activities operate

look.title: Children's Hours Under the 1833 Act
look.unit: hours per day in textile mills
look.cite: Factory Act of 1833 (UK Parliament, Living Heritage)
look.prompt: How did the rules change as children got older? Why might lawmakers draw lines by age?

check.q: What did the Factory Act of 1833 create to enforce the rules?
check.why: The 1833 act created paid factory inspectors to visit mills.

check.q: What did the Mines Act of 1842 ban?
choices: Women, girls and boys under ten working underground
check.why: The Mines Act banned women, girls and boys under ten from underground work.

check.q: What argument did opponents of the Factory Acts make?
choices: The laws interfered with free contracts and could hurt families needing wages
The laws did not go far enough to protect nobles
The laws gave children the vote
check.why: Opponents said the laws interfered with free contracts, raised costs and could hurt families.

sections.title: Big Ideas About Work and Wealth

lessons.title: Marx and Engels
lessons.mainIdea: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels argued in 1848 that history is a struggle between classes and that workers would overthrow capitalism.
reading: Friedrich Engels was the son of a German factory owner. In the 1840s he worked at his family's mill business in Manchester. He walked the city's poorest streets and wrote a book in 1845 about the lives of English workers. He became close friends with Karl Marx, a German philosopher and journalist.

In 1848 the two published The Communist Manifesto. They argued that all history is a story of *class struggle*, fights between those who own and those who work. Under *capitalism*, they said, owners of factories profit from workers' labor. They predicted that workers would rise up and create a society with no private ownership of factories, which they called communism.

Supporters over the years have said Marx and Engels saw real suffering and real inequality clearly. Their ideas inspired labor parties and movements for workers' rights. The Manifesto ends with a call: 'Working men of all countries, unite!'

words.d: Marx's idea that history is driven by conflict between social classes
an economic system in which private people own businesses and trade freely for profit
the idea of a society where property is owned in common and there are no social classes

look.title: The Opening Claim
look.text: The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.
look.cite: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, The Communist Manifesto, 1848 (English translation by Samuel Moore, 1888)
look.prompt: 'Hitherto existing' means 'that has existed until now.' Put this sentence in your own words.

check.q: When was The Communist Manifesto published?
check.why: Marx and Engels published the Manifesto in 1848.

check.q: What is 'class struggle' in Marx's view?
choices: Conflict between classes that drives history
check.why: Marx argued history is driven by conflict between those who own and those who work.

check.q: Where did Engels observe workers' lives in the 1840s?
check.why: Engels worked in Manchester and wrote about English workers in 1845.

lessons.title: Marx's Critics and the Record
lessons.mainIdea: Critics say Marx's predictions failed and that states built in his name caused mass suffering; supporters defend parts of his analysis.
reading: Marx predicted that workers' revolutions would come first in the most industrial countries, like Britain and Germany. That did not happen. Instead, in Britain and elsewhere, workers' wages rose over time, and many workers won the vote and joined unions and parties that worked through elections.

In the 1900s, governments that called themselves communist took power, starting with Russia in 1917. They seized private property and ruled as one-party states. Under Joseph Stalin, millions were sent to the Gulag, a system of forced labor camps. In China, the Great Leap Forward of 1958–62 led to a famine in which tens of millions died. In Cambodia, the Khmer Rouge killed or starved over a million people in the 1970s.

Critics, such as the economist Friedrich Hayek, argued that giving the state control over the economy leads to loss of freedom. Some defenders of Marx reply that these states twisted his ideas. Others value his critique of inequality but reject revolution. This remains a real debate, and you can weigh the evidence yourself.

words.d: the system of forced labor camps in the Soviet Union
a country where only one political party is allowed to hold power

look.title: Weighing a Theory
look.text: Claim: Marx predicted revolution in the most industrial countries. Evidence 1: Britain never had a communist revolution. Evidence 2: Russia, a mostly farming country, did in 1917. Evidence 3: British workers' wages rose over the 1800s.
look.prompt: Does this evidence support or weaken Marx's prediction? Explain using at least two pieces of evidence.

check.q: What was the Gulag?
choices: A system of forced labor camps in the Soviet Union
check.why: The Gulag was the Soviet system of forced labor camps under Stalin.

check.q: Which prediction of Marx did not come true?
choices: Revolution first in the most industrial countries
check.why: Marx expected revolutions in industrial Britain and Germany, but they did not happen there.

check.q: What was Hayek's main criticism?
choices: State control of the economy leads to loss of freedom
check.why: Hayek argued that state control of the economy threatens freedom.

lessons.title: Adam Smith and Free Markets
lessons.mainIdea: Adam Smith argued in 1776 that free markets and the division of labor create wealth, while also warning about their costs.
reading: Long before Marx, a Scottish professor named Adam Smith visited a small pin factory. He saw that when ten workers each did one step, like drawing wire or sharpening points, together they made tens of thousands of pins a day. One worker alone might make only a few. Splitting a job into small steps is called the *division of labor*.

In 1776, Smith published The Wealth of Nations. He argued that when people are free to trade, each person seeking their own gain can end up helping others. A baker bakes good bread to earn a living, and the town gets bread. Smith called this guiding force an 'invisible hand'. His ideas became the basis for *free-market* economics.

Smith was not only a cheerleader for business. He warned that merchants often plot to raise prices. He also worried that doing one tiny task all day could dull workers' minds, and he supported public schooling for them. Supporters credit free markets with lifting billions out of poverty. Critics say markets alone leave too many behind.

words.d: splitting a job into small steps, with each worker doing one step
an economy where prices and production are set mainly by buyers and sellers, not the government
Adam Smith's image for how people seeking their own gain in markets can end up helping others

look.title: The Butcher and the Baker
look.text: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker, that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
look.cite: Adam Smith, An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations, Book I, 1776
look.prompt: Benevolence means kindness. What is Smith saying about why the baker makes bread?

check.q: What did Smith observe in the pin factory?
choices: Pins were made only by hand at home
Dividing work into steps greatly raised output
check.why: Smith saw that ten workers each doing one step could make tens of thousands of pins a day.

check.q: What did Smith mean by the 'invisible hand'?
choices: People seeking their own gain in markets can end up helping others
check.why: The invisible hand is Smith's image for self-interest in free markets benefiting others.

check.q: Which warning did Smith himself give?
choices: Doing one tiny task all day could dull workers' minds
check.why: Smith worried that the division of labor could dull workers' minds and supported schooling for them.

lessons.title: Bismarck's Welfare State
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1880s Germany under Otto von Bismarck created the first national social insurance for workers.
reading: Otto von Bismarck was the powerful chancellor, or chief minister, of Germany. He was a conservative who disliked socialism. Yet in the 1880s he made Germany the first country to give workers national insurance. Health insurance came in 1883, accident insurance in 1884, and old-age and disability pensions in 1889.

This was a new idea: the government would help protect workers against sickness, injury and old age. Workers, employers and the state all paid in. A system where the government provides this kind of protection is called a *welfare state*. The insurance itself is called *social insurance*.

Bismarck's reasons were mixed. He hoped to win workers' loyalty away from the socialists, whom he also tried to ban. Supporters of welfare states say they reduce hardship and make life more secure. Critics warn that they can be costly and can weaken self-reliance. Many European countries later built their own versions.

words.d: a system in which the government helps protect people against sickness, injury, old age and poverty
a program where workers, employers or the state pay in, and people receive help when sick, injured or old
the chief minister of the government in Germany

look.title: Germany's First Social Insurance Laws
look.cite: German social insurance laws; see Social Security Administration, 'Otto von Bismarck' (history page)
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first and the last of these laws?

check.q: What was the first social insurance law Bismarck passed?
check.why: Health insurance came first, in 1883.

check.q: Why did Bismarck, a conservative, create social insurance?
choices: To win workers' loyalty away from socialists
check.why: He hoped to draw workers away from the socialists.

check.q: What is a welfare state?
choices: Government protection against sickness, injury and old age
check.why: A welfare state is one where the government helps protect people against such risks.

review.q: Where and when did the Industrial Revolution begin?
review.why: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain from about the 1760s.

review.q: What was a piecer's job in a cotton mill?
choices: Inspecting the factory for the government

review.why: In the story, Mary twists broken threads together on the spinning mule.

review.q: Which group grew as factory owners, merchants and professionals prospered?
review.why: Factory owners, merchants and professionals formed the growing middle class.

review.q: How did the Factory Act of 1833 try to make sure its rules were followed?
review.why: The act created paid inspectors, because earlier laws were not checked.

review.q: How do Adam Smith and Karl Marx differ?
choices: Both wanted to abolish private property
Smith saw free markets creating wealth; Marx saw capitalism as exploiting workers
Smith wanted revolution; Marx praised the invisible hand
review.why: Smith argued free markets create wealth; Marx argued owners profit from workers' labor.

review.q: What is one piece of evidence critics use against communist states?
choices: The Great Leap Forward famine in China
review.why: The Great Leap Forward led to a famine in which tens of millions died.

review.q: Which country first created national social insurance in the 1880s?
review.why: Germany under Bismarck passed health, accident and pension laws in the 1880s.

review.q: Why did workers form trade unions?
choices: To bargain together for better pay and conditions
review.why: Unions let workers bargain together, giving them more power than one worker alone.
